title: Load Balancing
subtitle: One address, many machines — and who decides where your request goes
objectives: Explain what a load balancer buys you, and why it's indirection rather than speed
Choose a distribution algorithm based on whether requests and servers are uniform
Describe how health checks fail — including evicting healthy machines under load
Reason about the balancer as its own single point of failure, L4 vs L7, and why sticky sessions are a smell

exercises.title: What a load balancer really sells is indirection
exercises.body: Users can't be asked to know your machines. So one thing sits out front, owns the single address the world talks to, and hands each request to a server behind it. That's a load balancer. The distribution is the obvious part; the valuable part is that the outside now talks to one stable thing instead of to your servers.
exercises.note: The address is where your promises to the world stop and your freedom starts. Outside it, one name that never changes. Inside it, an arrangement that is nobody's business but yours.

exercises.prompt: You now run 3 identical app servers. Your users only know one address. What has to exist?
choices: Something in front that receives every request and picks a server to hand it to
The servers must merge into one machine
Each user must be given a different address
exercises.why: Users can't be asked to know your machines, so something must present one address to the world and route each request behind it. That's a load balancer — and what it really sells is indirection: because the outside world talks to one stable thing, you can add, remove, restart, and replace machines behind it all day without anyone noticing. Every machine becoming disposable is what horizontal scaling actually cashes in.

exercises.prompt: A ______ balancer presents one address to clients and distributes requests across many servers.
exercises.why: One front door, many rooms behind it — and the clients never learn how many rooms there are.

exercises.prompt: Match each thing a load balancer gives you.

pairs.right: Clients don't know or care how many servers exist
A server can finish its work before leaving

exercises.why: Distribution is the obvious job, but the other three are what you'll actually think about day to day. Most people describe a load balancer as 'it spreads traffic'; in practice it's the stable address, the removal of dead machines, and graceful departure that let you deploy on a Tuesday afternoon without anyone noticing.

exercises.prompt: Beyond spreading load, what does a load balancer let you do that's arguably more valuable day to day?
choices: Take a server out of rotation — to deploy, patch, or replace it — without downtime
exercises.why: If traffic can be moved off a machine at will, that machine can be upgraded or destroyed whenever you like, so deploys become routine instead of events. This is why balancers appear even in systems whose traffic one server could handle: you're often not buying capacity at all, you're buying the ability to take a machine away safely.

exercises.prompt: Your load balancer sends requests to 3 servers. One is much slower than the others — but it's not down. What does the LB do about it?
choices: Nothing automatically — 'slow' isn't 'dead', and a basic health check only asks whether it responds
It sends the request to all three
exercises.why: A basic health check asks a yes/no question — are you answering? — and a server answering slowly passes it and keeps taking traffic. That gap between 'up' and 'healthy' is where a lot of real pain lives: a machine responding in 8 seconds is often worse for users than one that's cleanly dead, because a dead one gets removed and a slow one keeps accepting their requests.

exercises.prompt: What does adding a load balancer NOT do?
choices: Give you one address for many servers
Let you remove a server without downtime
Stop sending traffic to a dead server
exercises.why: It routes; it doesn't compute. A single request does exactly the work it always did, plus one extra network hop to get there — so you've slightly increased latency to buy capacity and disposable machines. That's unit 4's throughput-versus-latency trade, made concrete in a box.

exercises.title: Every balancing algorithm is an assumption about your traffic wearing a name
exercises.body: Something must pick a server for every request, and no rule for picking is neutral — each one is a bet about your traffic, made once in a config file and then never looked at again. *Round robin* is the plain one: A, then B, then C, then A. It takes turns, so it spreads request COUNTS across the pool perfectly evenly. Perfectly.
exercises.note: So the useful question about an algorithm isn't what it does — that's one sentence — it's what it refuses to look at. Round robin looks at nothing: not the server, not the request, not its own last decision. It counts.

exercises.prompt: The simplest algorithm: send request 1 to server A, request 2 to B, request 3 to C, then back to A. What's it called, and what does it quietly assume?
choices: Least connections — it assumes servers are identical
Round robin — it assumes every request costs about the same
Hashing — it assumes users are evenly spread
exercises.why: Round robin takes turns, which distributes request COUNTS evenly — and that only distributes LOAD evenly when requests cost about the same. If one request in fifty is a report that takes 30 seconds while the rest take 5ms, taking turns will cheerfully deal three reports onto one machine while the others idle.

exercises.prompt: Match each algorithm to what it does.

pairs.right: Send to whoever is currently least busy
Bigger servers get a larger share
The same key always lands on the same server

exercises.why: Four strategies for four situations: uniform requests, uneven requests, uneven servers, and requests that need to land somewhere specific. Notice only the last is about WHERE a request goes rather than how busy a server is — hashing exists for when the destination matters, which is a different problem from balancing.

exercises.prompt: Your requests vary wildly: most take 5ms, some take 30 seconds. Which algorithm handles that better?
choices: Least connections — it notices a server is still busy with a slow request and routes around it
exercises.why: Least connections uses live evidence: a machine stuck on a 30-second request still shows an open connection, so it stops receiving new work, while round robin has no idea and keeps dealing it cards. The general principle is that round robin is open-loop — it never looks at the result — and least-connections is closed-loop. Uniform workloads make that feedback nearly worthless; the more variance you have, the more it's worth.

exercises.prompt: Your fleet has a mix: some machines have 8 cores, some have 32. Which approach fits?
choices: Weighted — give the bigger machines a proportionally larger share
exercises.why: Equal shares to unequal machines overloads the small ones while the big ones coast, so weights let you say 'this one takes four times as much.' The catch is that a weight is a number a human guessed and then forgot, and it drifts out of date as hardware and workloads change — which is a real part of why homogeneous fleets are popular. Uniformity isn't elegant, it just deletes a config nobody maintains.

exercises.prompt: Why might you hash a user's id to pick their server, instead of balancing by load?
choices: Because you want that user to land on the same server repeatedly — for a warm local cache, say
It spreads load more evenly than round robin
exercises.why: Hashing trades load-balancing quality for predictable placement: the same key reaches the same server every time, so whatever that server cached for them is still there. The cost is that you've deliberately made servers non-interchangeable — the very property unit 11 said horizontal scaling depends on — so losing a server now loses something, and adding one reshuffles who goes where.

exercises.prompt: Which algorithm is 'best'?
choices: None: it depends on whether requests cost the same, whether servers are the same, and whether placement matters
exercises.why: Three questions decide it — are requests uniform, are servers uniform, does it matter where a request lands — and once you answer them the algorithm mostly picks itself. Round robin is a very common default and a reasonable one, since uniform-ish requests on uniform servers is genuinely common; just know it was chosen for simplicity rather than as a verdict about your workload, so it's the first thing to revisit when your request costs get lumpy.

exercises.title: A dead server can't tell you it died, so the balancer never stops asking
exercises.body: Nothing announces its own crash. So the balancer probes every server on a schedule — a `GET /health` every few seconds — and pulls whichever stop answering out of rotation. That's an *active* health check. The passive alternative watches real traffic and notices the failures, which costs no probes but only ever learns by hurting real users first.
exercises.note: The probe asks a yes/no question: are you answering? So a server replying in 800ms passes and keeps taking your users' requests. *Up* and *healthy* are not the same word, and that gap is where this lesson lives.

exercises.prompt: How does the load balancer know a server has died?
choices: The server tells it before crashing
It checks — periodically asking each server whether it's alive, and removing those that fail
It doesn't; an engineer has to remove it
exercises.why: Dead machines can't announce anything, so the balancer has to keep asking. That's an active health check — probing an endpoint like `/health` on a schedule. The alternative is passive: watch real traffic and notice failures, which costs nothing extra but only learns by hurting real users first, whereas active spends probes to find out before anyone gets hurt.

exercises.prompt: Your `/health` endpoint just returns `200 OK` unconditionally. What's the problem?
choices: Nothing — it proves the server is up
It proves the web server can answer, not that the app can do its job — a server with a dead database connection passes happily
exercises.why: A hardcoded 200 tests one thing: the process is running and can serve a route. It says nothing about whether this server can fulfil a real request. So a good check exercises the dependencies the server truly needs — but don't over-swing, because if your check queries the database then one database blip fails the check on every server at once and the balancer dutifully removes your entire fleet. Too shallow keeps broken servers; too deep takes everything out together.

exercises.prompt: Under heavy load your servers get slow, so health checks start timing out. The LB removes those servers. What happens next?
choices: The remaining servers get the same traffic across fewer machines, so they get slower and fail checks too — the fleet unravels one machine at a time
exercises.why: You removed capacity from an overloaded system: the load didn't leave, it redistributed onto fewer machines and pushed them over the same line, one after another. That's a cascading failure, and the bitter part is the health check did exactly what it was told — a slow-but-working server was worth keeping, and the check couldn't tell 'overloaded' from 'broken.' Some balancers guard against this with a floor that never removes more than a set fraction of the pool, precisely because 'everything looks unhealthy at once' more often means overload than mass death.

exercises.prompt: Which are real risks of health check configuration? Select all.
choices: Too shallow: broken servers keep serving traffic
Too deep: one shared dependency failing removes the entire fleet at once
Too aggressive: brief slowness under load evicts healthy machines
exercises.why: Shallow, deep, and aggressive are all real failure modes, and they pull against each other — so you're tuning between them rather than eliminating them. Checking many servers is just work the balancer does. Every one of these is the same 'is it dead or just slow?' question from the replication unit in different clothes: you can't answer it from outside, so you're choosing which mistake to make — keep a broken server, or evict a healthy one.

exercises.prompt: You're deploying. You want to stop sending new requests to a server but let it finish the ones it's already handling. What's that called?
exercises.why: Draining stops new traffic while in-flight requests complete, so nobody eats an error just because you deployed. Skipping it is why so many deploys produce a small spike of 502s — the machine vanished mid-request — and it's the difference between deploys nobody notices and deploys that quietly fail a few hundred people every time, for years, because nobody looks at a spike that small.

exercises.prompt: A server that failed its health check recovers and rejoins the pool. What's the risk?
choices: It can be handed a rush of traffic before it's warmed up — cold caches, empty connection pools — and immediately fall over again
exercises.why: A freshly-started server looks identical to a warm one from outside, but nothing's cached and nothing's connected — so a full share dealt instantly can buckle it straight back out of the pool. The mitigation is slow start: ramp a returning server's share up over some seconds instead of dealing it a full hand, which turns a flapping loop of join-die-join-die into an uneventful recovery.

exercises.title: A single point of failure is something you relocate, not something you delete
exercises.body: Every request now flows through one box. Real setups run several balancers and share the address between them — DNS handing out multiple IPs, a floating IP that jumps to a standby, or anycast. None of those deletes the last shared thing; they shrink it and shorten how long it's broken. The question is never *whether*, but *where, and how fast it's replaced*.
exercises.note: Notice where those mitigations live: not one of them is inside the balancer. Each pushes the shared thing further out — into DNS, into a routing table — until what's left is small and dumb enough to be trusted.

exercises.prompt: You put a load balancer in front of your servers so no single machine can take you down. Then the load balancer dies. What have you built?
choices: A new single point of failure — you moved it rather than removed it
exercises.why: Everything now flows through one box, so its death is total — precisely the property you added it to fix. The honest framing is that you don't remove single points of failure so much as push them somewhere you can afford: real setups run multiple balancers, via DNS handing out several addresses, a floating IP that moves between them, or anycast. The question is never 'is there a SPOF?' but 'where is it, and how fast can it be replaced?'

exercises.prompt: Match each load balancer type to what it can do.

pairs.right: Routes by IP and port, without reading the request
Reads the HTTP request — can route by path or header

exercises.why: L4 moves packets between addresses without opening them; L7 understands HTTP, so it can send /api one way and /images another, and pays overhead for the privilege of understanding. The tell for which you need: are you routing on anything INSIDE the request — path, host, header, cookie? That's L7, because L4 literally cannot see those. If you're just spreading connections across identical servers, L4 does it with less machinery.

exercises.prompt: Sessions live in each server's local memory, so users break when they land on a different machine. Someone suggests sticky sessions — pinning each user to one server. Is that a fix?
choices: It's a workaround: it hides the symptom by making your servers non-interchangeable, which is the property you were relying on
Yes, and it also improves load distribution
exercises.why: Sticky sessions work by giving up interchangeability — the session still exists in exactly one place, you've just arranged for the user to keep going back to it. So you inherit what that implies: that server dying logs those users out, load distributes worse because a machine with heavy users stays hot, and draining for a deploy pushes people off their sessions anyway. Moving session state out of local memory (unit 5) fixes the cause instead of the symptom.

exercises.prompt: Your app keeps sessions in local server memory and it's hurting. Slide toward your approach.
exercises.rightLabel: Move sessions to a shared store (real fix, more work)
exercises.why: Sticky sessions buy you today at the cost of every day after: servers stay non-interchangeable, so deploys, failures, and autoscaling all keep hurting. They're defensible as a deliberate stopgap while you do the real work, or for something genuinely local and cheap to lose. What makes them a smell is being load-bearing forever — at that point your architecture has quietly decided machines aren't disposable, and everything downstream gets harder.

exercises.prompt: A load balancer distributes traffic across servers. So can it protect you from a traffic spike bigger than your whole fleet can handle?
choices: No — it spreads load; it doesn't reduce it. Distributing 10× traffic across 3 servers just overloads all 3 evenly
Yes, it queues the extra requests forever
Yes, if you use least connections
exercises.why: Balancing decides who does the work, not how much work exists — so if the total exceeds your fleet's capacity, spreading it perfectly still exceeds your fleet's capacity. Protection from too much load is a different tool entirely: shedding it (rejecting early with a 429, unit 2), limiting it, or adding capacity. Confusing 'balanced' with 'protected' is a common and expensive mistake, because an evenly overloaded fleet is still an overloaded fleet.

exercises.prompt: Users report intermittent errors during every deploy. You use round robin, no draining, and health checks every 30 seconds. What's the most likely cause?
choices: Round robin is the wrong algorithm
Servers are being killed mid-request, and for up to 30 seconds the LB keeps sending traffic to machines that are already gone
exercises.why: Two gaps compound: no draining means in-flight requests die with the process, and a 30-second interval means the balancer keeps confidently routing to a dead machine until its next probe. The interval is a tradeoff you're making whether you notice or not — probe often and you spend requests while risking eviction on a blip; probe rarely and you feed traffic to corpses. Draining is what makes the interval mostly stop mattering, because the machine leaves on purpose instead of being discovered missing.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of load balancing?
choices: It makes your system fast and highly available automatically
It gives you one address and disposable machines — and hands you new decisions: which algorithm, how to check health, and where the single point of failure moved to
It's only needed above a million users
It removes the need for health checks
exercises.why: It's the component that makes a fleet usable as one service, and it doesn't reduce load, speed up requests, or remove failure — it relocates and manages them. Look at what it actually delivered: not capacity (the servers did that) and not speed (nothing got faster), but indirection, which bought disposable machines. Almost every operational nicety you like about running a fleet traces back to that one thing.
